source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-ended wargames with large language models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe automates open-ended (qualitative) wargames with LLM agents: a control agent (adjudicator), players with personas, and teams. Zero-shot, no fine-tuning. Earlier LLM wargames allowed only fixed move menus.
numbers: Mistral-7B-OpenOrca was the best small open model; output is randomised so no two runs match. Prior LLM wargames allowed 7, 27, or 21 binary discrete moves.
limits: Architecture paper, not validated against real outcomes. No human baseline.
agent_relevance: Shows the role split we want: program owns turn order and history, model fills slots (player move, adjudication). Matches the schema's program/model split.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-ended wargames with large language models (Snow Globe)
finding: A three-word prompt addition, 'Include unexpected consequences', made the LLM adjudicator generate 'nature' (events nobody ordered). Authors say the common adjudication faults are repeated output across moves and hallucinated player plans.
numbers: Prompt change: 3 words. No effect size reported.
quote: Hallucination, which in other applications is so often harmful, is the key to making open-ended LLM wargames work.
limits: Anecdotal. No measured rate for the faults.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt lever for a simulated-evaluation step. The two failure modes (repetition, invented plans) are what code checks should catch.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-ended wargames with large language models (Snow Globe)
finding: Persona manipulation changed outcomes in a two-state crisis: more hawk personas gave more armed conflict. Authors argue repeated randomised runs can reveal links between policy, persona and outcome.
numbers: Armed conflict in 20 runs per cell: dove-dove 1/20, dove-hawk 4/20, hawk-hawk 14/20.
limits: Small N (20 per cell), one scenario, one 7B model. Authors warn against trusting raw probabilities. Conflicts with Lamparth 2024 on persona sensitivity (different models, real expert baseline).
agent_relevance: Persona effects depend on model and setup. Do not use persona voters (G4); test sensitivity by running.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: generative pre-trained transformers for accelerated course of action development
finding: COA-GPT gives an LLM mission text (plus an image in the -V variant) and doctrine excerpts; it proposes several named COAs in seconds. A commander gives natural-language feedback and the COA is refined. COAs are scored by running them in a militarised StarCraft II scenario.
numbers: 5 COAs per variant x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts per method. Expert human: 15 trials. The Autocurriculum RL baseline needed 112 thousand simulated battles, 70 million timesteps, 35 workers.
limits: One scenario. Game is mostly deterministic, so variance comes from COA diversity. RL baseline numbers were copied from the original paper, not re-run.
agent_relevance: A direct case of test-by-running: generate plan, execute in simulator, score. COAs came in seconds with no retraining.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: generative pre-trained transformers for accelerated course of action development
finding: With no human feedback COA-GPT beat the RL baselines on mean total reward. One or two rounds of human feedback raised mean reward and cut variance. The best vision variant was 3.4% below the expert human on mean score, but the human had larger variance.
numbers: Best COA-GPT-V+H1/H2 mean reward 3.4% lower than the expert human (15 trials). COA-GPT had higher friendly casualties than all baselines; the human had the lowest friendly and highest hostile casualties.
limits: Feedback came from the authors' own process. Human N=15. Single scenario. Higher casualties blamed on one-shot command with no mid-episode control.
agent_relevance: Feedback grounded in simulated outcomes improves the plan (supports G2). A plan fixed at the start loses to continuous control.

source: Rivera, Mukobi, Reuel, Lamparth, Smith, Schneider (2024) Escalation risks from language models in military and diplomatic decision-making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents (one model per run) played turn-based wargames; a separate world-model LLM wrote the consequences. All five models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base) showed statistically significant initial escalation. None showed significant de-escalation over the game.
numbers: 5 models x 3 scenarios (neutral, invasion, cyberattack) x 10 simulations x 8 agents. GPT-3.5 escalation score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario.
limits: Nation profiles and scoring weights were set by the authors. The world model is itself an LLM. No human arm was run. Elbaum & Panter 2025 show prompts and temperature move the result a lot.
agent_relevance: Self-play of one model on all sides escalates and shows arms-race dynamics. Same-model sides are not independent opposition (G4, G9).

source: Rivera, Mukobi, Reuel, Lamparth, Smith, Schneider (2024) Escalation risks from language models in military and diplomatic decision-making
finding: Military capacity rose steadily in all models and scenarios (arms-race dynamics). Escalation spiked suddenly and unpredictably, some runs by over 50% in one turn. Rare nuclear use occurred, with deterrence and first-strike reasoning in the chain-of-thought.
numbers: GPT-4-Base (no RLHF) executed nuclear strikes about 2.48 per nation versus 7.38 messages per nation (about 33% as often).
quote: A lot of countries have nuclear weapons... We have it! Let's use it.
limits: GPT-4-Base is not a deployed model and the authors say it is unrepresentative. Reasoning text records, but does not prove, the cause (G10).
agent_relevance: Written reasoning justified severe actions. Treat it as unreliable evidence. Base-model-like behaviour appears when safety tuning is missing.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. machine: behavioral differences between expert humans and language models in wargame simulations
finding: First direct comparison of expert human teams with LLM-simulated teams on the same fictional US-China Taiwan Strait crisis. Coarse agreement was high, but there were systematic differences in individual actions and strategic tendencies.
numbers: 214 national-security experts in 48 teams vs GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Of 21 possible actions, LLM frequency statistically matched humans on 16 (GPT-3.5), 10 (GPT-4), 9 (GPT-4o).
limits: Two-move game with a fixed 21-action menu. US-biased sample. An earlier preprint version had fewer experts. Match counts depend on the test used.
agent_relevance: A simulated evaluator can match experts on the coarse pattern and miss specifics. Coarse agreement is a hint, not proof.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. machine: behavioral differences between expert humans and language models in wargame simulations
finding: Treatment effects (AI-weapon accuracy, crew training, China posture) mostly gave the same significance pattern in LLM runs as in human runs (Table 1).
numbers: Statistical conclusions from LLM experiments 'mostly consistent' with human trials across three treatment variables.
limits: Not every treatment matched across models. One scenario.
agent_relevance: Simulated runs are better for comparing conditions (plan A vs plan B) than for predicting absolute outcomes.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. machine: behavioral differences between expert humans and language models in wargame simulations
finding: Prompt design changed results. Asking the LLM to simulate a dialogue between team members made choices more aggressive and closer to human aggressiveness (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) but raised the number of actions chosen, away from humans. The simulated dialogue lacked disagreement.
numbers: Dialogue length varied in chunks of about 350 words; final comparisons used three chunks. Direct answer vs simulated dialogue differed for all models.
quote: the simulated players exclusively give short statements and rarely disagree with each other
limits: GPT-4o became more aggressive than humans with more dialogue. No single setting matched humans on both measures.
agent_relevance: Multi-voice role-play inside one model gives fake disagreement. Supports G9 (no debate) and G4 (no persona voters).

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. machine: behavioral differences between expert humans and language models in wargame simulations
finding: LLM teams ignored player background. Describing all players as 'strict pacifists' or 'aggressive sociopaths' gave no significant difference in either move for any model. Adding the President's three priorities changed GPT-3.5 (more 'Fire at Chinese vessels') but for GPT-4 only reduced the hold-fire options.
numbers: Extreme personas tested on all three models, both moves: no significant difference. Move-2 consistency: p(aggressive in move 2 given de-escalatory move 1) was lower for GPT-4 and humans than for GPT-3.5.
limits: Contrasts with Hogan & Brennen 2024, where hawk/dove personas shifted conflict. Differences may come from model, team framing or action menu.
agent_relevance: Personas are weak levers on simulated teams. Instruction priorities work unevenly across models.

source: Hua et al. (2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based multi-agent simulation of world wars
finding: WarAgent simulates countries as LLM agents. Each has a secretary agent that checks the proposed action for format and logical consistency. Run on WWI, WWII and Warring States China. Alliance and mobilisation accuracy were high; war-declaration accuracy was low. A world war broke out in every simulation.
numbers: Default (anonymised) setting: alliance accuracy over 75%, mobilisation over 90%, war declarations low. 7 simulations per setting.
limits: Only 7 runs. Scored against one historical record. 'War always breaks out' is a bias, not a prediction.
agent_relevance: The secretary is a separate checking step on a plan, like our checks, but it is an LLM check.

source: Hua et al. (2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based multi-agent simulation of world wars
finding: Reasoning versus recall test: de-anonymised runs (real country names, told to replicate history) matched history on alliance and mobilisation and were consistent across models and seeds, which points to memory. Anonymised runs varied by model and seed.
numbers: De-anonymised WWI: alliance accuracy 97.43% for GPT-4, Claude-2 and GPT-3.5; mobilisation 100%; war-declaration accuracy only about 13-19%.
limits: War declarations scored poorly because agents listed all wars of the whole conflict.
agent_relevance: Real names in a historical scenario leak the answer. Anonymise to test reasoning (G3).

source: Hua et al. (2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based multi-agent simulation of world wars
finding: Counterfactual fine-tuning (108 data points, 3 epochs, GPT-3.5 told WWI never happened) did not stop the simulated world war.
numbers: Before vs after: alliance 43.38 vs 31.02; war declaration 7.83 vs 15.18; mobilisation 78.06 vs 62.12 (as read from a garbled PDF table).
limits: Only 108 items. GPT-3.5 reasoning also degraded. The authors' reading, that the sim does not just recall training data, is weak.
agent_relevance: A sim that always reaches the same outcome whatever the knowledge is biased. Do not trust it as a predictor.

source: Elbaum & Panter (2025) Managing escalation in off-the-shelf large language models
finding: Two cheap interventions cut escalation in the Rivera et al. wargame run with Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3: lower temperature and reflection prompts. The planning reflection cut average escalation 28%; the de-escalation reflection cut it 57%.
numbers: 10 runs per treatment. Mean escalation per nation: 6.37 at T=1.0; 3.96 at 0.5 (-38%); 3.33 at 0.01 (-48%); planning reflection 4.61; de-escalation reflection 2.76; 50-word RAND context prompt -8%. Violent escalation fell over 80%; nuclear actions fell from 0.08 per nation to zero with the de-escalation reflection.
quote: reflection (planning) prompt reduced the average score by 28%
limits: One small model, one scenario, 10 runs. The de-escalation prompt tells the model what to do, so it partly measures instruction following. The context prompt was too short to show an effect.
agent_relevance: A private-thought slot under 250 words before acting changes behaviour. But the effect is on the escalation score, not on plan quality.

source: Payne (2026) AI arms and influence: frontier models exhibit sophisticated reasoning in simulated nuclear crises
finding: Three frontier models (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 3 Flash) played each other in a nuclear-crisis tournament. All games had nuclear signalling. No model chose accommodation or withdrawal. Threats more often provoked counter-escalation than compliance.
numbers: 21 games, 329 turns, 780,000 words. None of the eight de-escalatory options (-5 to -95) was chosen; the mildest action chosen was 'Return to Start Line' (0), 45 times (6.9%). 95% of games had mutual nuclear signalling. Tactical nuclear use in 86% (Claude), 79% (Gemini), 64% (GPT-5.2) of games.
limits: Single-author preprint. The escalation ladder and an accident mechanic are the author's design. Deadlines are scenario content, not a clean treatment (author says so).
agent_relevance: A simulated adversary built from the same model class never concedes. An evaluator that cannot retreat biases plan tests.

source: Payne (2026) AI arms and influence: frontier models exhibit sophisticated reasoning in simulated nuclear crises
finding: Behaviour flipped with a time limit. Claude won 100% of open-ended games but 33% under deadline; GPT-5.2 went from 0% to 75%. GPT-5.2 median escalation rose from 175 to 900 under deadline.
numbers: 9 open-ended and 12 deadline games. Overall: Claude 8-4 (67%), GPT-5.2 6-6 (50%), Gemini 4-8 (33%). GPT-5.2 crossed the tactical nuclear line in 17% of open-ended games and 100% of deadline games.
limits: Deadline embedded in scenario design; very small N per cell.
agent_relevance: A model's behaviour is framing-dependent. Test a plan under several framings, not one.

source: Payne (2026) AI arms and influence: frontier models exhibit sophisticated reasoning in simulated nuclear crises
finding: Models misjudged opponents when the framing changed. Mental models that worked in open play became liabilities under deadline pressure. Stated signals matched later actions only about 70% of the time.
numbers: Signal-action match about 70% on average. One model acted more aggressively than announced in 70% of mid-level and 60% of high-level moves.
limits: Descriptive. Based on logs and model self-reports.
agent_relevance: The model's stated intent is a poor guide to what it will do (G10).

source: Jensen, Reynolds, Atalan, Garcia, Woo, Chen, Howarth (2025) Critical Foreign Policy Decisions (CFPD)-Benchmark
finding: A benchmark avoids running a full wargame: 400 expert-written scenarios (100 each for escalation, intervention, cooperation, alliance) with swappable country actors give 66,473 questions. Among seven models, Qwen2 72B, Gemini 1.5 Pro-002 and Llama 3.1 8B were more escalatory than Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o.
numbers: 7 models, 400 scenarios, 66,473 questions, bootstrap 95% CI. GPT-4o was least escalatory and significantly different from Qwen2 72B and Llama 3.1 8B.
limits: No ground truth by design. Measures preference, not accuracy. Gemini 1.5 escalated in two-choice but not three-choice versions, so the option set changes answers.
agent_relevance: Adding a middle option changed the model's choice, so check plans against several option formats. Batch scenarios are easier to repeat than agentic wargames.

source: Jensen, Reynolds, Atalan, Garcia, Woo, Chen, Howarth (2025) Critical Foreign Policy Decisions (CFPD)-Benchmark
finding: All seven models showed country-specific bias: less escalatory and interventionist recommendations for China and Russia than for the US and UK.
numbers: Swapped actors across the same 400 scenarios; differences reported with bootstrap CI.
limits: Authors cite contamination concerns and do not re-run newer models.
agent_relevance: Actor names alone shift the verdict. Anonymise actors when scoring a plan (same lesson as WarAgent).

source: Shrivastava, Hullman, Lamparth (2024) Measuring free-form decision-making inconsistency of language models in military crisis simulations
finding: Free-form wargame answers differed in meaning across repeated samples for all five tested models, measured as 1 minus BERTScore (DeBERTa-xlarge-MNLI). Inconsistency stayed at lower temperature and after anonymising countries.
numbers: 5 LMs (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini least inconsistent, GPT-4 most. Temperatures 0.2 to 1.2: inconsistency fell with temperature but did not vanish. Anonymising countries had no significant effect.
limits: BERTScore is a proxy (validated with text ablations). Exact values are only in figures.
agent_relevance: One run of a simulated evaluator is noise. Run several and look at spread (G12).

source: Shrivastava, Hullman, Lamparth (2024) Measuring free-form decision-making inconsistency of language models in military crisis simulations
finding: Prompt wording moved answers as much as temperature. At T=0, meaning-preserving rewrites gave inconsistency comparable to T=0.2 for all models except GPT-4; meaning-changing edits gave inconsistency like T=0.6 to 0.8.
numbers: Meaning-preserving ablation about T=0.2; meaning-changing about T=0.6-0.8; GPT-3.5 Turbo an exception on the second.
limits: Claude excluded from temperature comparisons because its API temperature range differs.
agent_relevance: T=0 does not make an evaluator stable. Use paraphrase checks as a test of any simulated judge.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Large language models play StarCraft II: benchmarks and a chain of summarization approach
finding: TextStarCraft II turns the game into text. The Chain of Summarization (CoS) method compresses single-frame and multi-frame observations before the model acts. Most of ten LLMs beat the built-in level-5 AI; fine-tuned small models matched Gold-level human players.
numbers: Ten LLMs tested. Closed-source models beat the built-in level-5 AI. Un-fine-tuned Llama2 70B could not produce valid commands. Abstract: fine-tuned LLMs on par with Gold-level players.
limits: Scripted game opponent, few human matches, Gold is a mid-skill tier.
agent_relevance: A compression step before acting is a scaffold that moves wargame performance. The opponent is a simulator, so plans are scored by running.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Large language models play StarCraft II: benchmarks and a chain of summarization approach
finding: A structured thought-chain prompt (situation overview, analysis, planning, decision) multiplied win rates against harder built-in AI compared with a simple prompt.
numbers: Win rate by built-in difficulty, prompt 1 vs prompt 2: L1 87.5 vs 100; L2 66.7 vs 100; L3 25.0 vs 100; L4 12.5 vs 84; L5 0 vs 50; L6 0 vs 8.3 (GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, Protoss vs Zerg).
limits: One model, one match-up. Prompt 2 was written by experts and embeds domain knowledge.
agent_relevance: Domain-structured staged prompt gave large gains where the plain prompt had a foothold (L1-L3), as G12 predicts. At L6 both fail.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Large language models play StarCraft II: benchmarks and a chain of summarization approach
finding: Fine-tuning data quality mattered: training on wins from the top 25% of games by average population utilisation gave the best win rate; the full dataset did worse.
numbers: Win rate 54/100 (top-25% APU wins) vs 28/100 (full dataset).
limits: Distilled from GPT-3.5 logs, filtered by a proxy metric (APU).
agent_relevance: Selecting by a measured outcome beats using all attempts. Consistent with 'code selects' (G5).

source: Guan, Kong, Zhong, Wang (2024) Richelieu: self-evolving LLM-based agents for AI Diplomacy
finding: Richelieu is an LLM diplomacy agent with memory, reflection, forward-simulation of others' moves, and self-play to build experience without human data. Against AutoGPT agents it won far more.
numbers: Press Diplomacy vs AutoGPT (4 trials): Richelieu win 9.10%, most-supply-centres 18.33%, survived 38.27%, defeated 34.30%. AutoGPT: 1.63%, 4.10%, 32.90%, 61.37%.
limits: Absolute 7-player win rates are low. AutoGPT is a weak baseline.
agent_relevance: A planner that simulates others' replies and stores self-play outcomes in memory is a method from this field already inside an LLM agent loop.

source: Guan, Kong, Zhong, Wang (2024) Richelieu: self-evolving LLM-based agents for AI Diplomacy
finding: Against Cicero (trained on human games) in the press setting Richelieu was only marginally better. The authors say the win-rate gain is not significant.
numbers: Win rate about 0.7% higher, Most SC about 2% higher, defeated rate 0.6% lower; authors' own score about 10% higher. Averages 6.83% vs 6.03% win in one table.
limits: Differences small; many draws because 3-4 of 7 countries are the same agent. No significance test beyond the authors' remark.
agent_relevance: Self-play with the same model on several sides gives draws and small gains. Weak evidence for self-play memory.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) citing RAND Strategy Assessment System (RSAS) and Emery (2021)
finding: Cited by opened papers, not read here: the RAND Strategy Assessment System of the 1980s ran wargames with expert-system AI players. Emery (2021) reported that early computer-assisted wargames led to more nuclear use.
numbers: No numbers read directly.
limits: Secondhand through Hogan & Brennen and Lamparth et al.
agent_relevance: Older computational ancestor. The same escalation tilt in LLM sims may be a property of machine players in general.

source: Cranfield 'Intelligent wargaming approach' thesis and AIAA studies (from the SUBFIELDS row)
finding: Could not be opened (HTTP 403 from the repository; web search budget exhausted). The prior-pass note lists these as search-result-only items.
numbers: None.
limits: Unverified. Do not treat as evidence.
agent_relevance: Left as a lead only.
